report:
Conclusion: yes—but only modestly and inconsistently. For otherwise healthy women with recurrent uncomplicated cystitis, regular cranberry products appear to lower the risk of symptomatic, culture-confirmed recurrence rather than eliminate it. The 2023 Cochrane review concluded cranberry products probably reduce these UTIs in women with recurrent UTIs (about RR 0.74), while noting limits in certainty and applicability (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37068952/). A JAMA summary of the updated evidence similarly reports about a 26% risk reduction in women with recurrent UTIs, with stronger effects in some other groups (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2804706).

However, “cranberry” is not one standardized intervention: juice, cocktail, tablets/capsules and proanthocyanidin (PAC) dose vary widely, and a large placebo-controlled trial of cranberry juice found no prevention benefit (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3060891/). Reflecting this mixed evidence, the AUA says clinicians may offer cranberry prophylaxis to women with recurrent uncomplicated UTI, but evidence is insufficient to recommend one formulation over another (https://www.auanet.org/guidelines-and-quality/guidelines/recurrent-uti).

Practical takeaway: a standardized PAC-containing product is a reasonable low-risk adjunct for prevention, but sugary juice is not ideal, benefit is modest, and cranberry does not treat an active infection or replace evaluation/antibiotics when indicated.
